query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In rare‐earth‐free high‐entropy alloys, engineering a nanoscale dual-phase (or heterogeneous) microstructure creates local regions with distinct magnetic exchange interactions that enable a low-field induced, reversible magnetostructural transition. These interfaces both lower the energy barriers for domain reordering and act as efficient thermal conduction pathways, leading to an enhanced magnetocaloric effect at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and robust mechanical stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A rare‐earth‐free high‐entropy alloy initially prepared in a near-homogeneous single-phase state.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the cooling rate (or implement a post-synthesis annealing protocol) to induce controlled nanoscale dual-phase heterogeneity versus maintaining a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted near room temperature under low applied magnetic fields (e.g., < 1 T) on alloys with identical nominal compositions but differing microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale phase boundaries or interfaces between coexisting magnetic regions within the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Chemical disorder induces regions with slightly different magnetic coupling. At the nanoscale interfaces, lower energy barriers enable a reversible magnetostructural transition when a modest field is applied. These interfaces simultaneously promote efficient phonon transport for rapid heat exchange and minimize hysteresis by reducing pinning effects, while preserving mechanical integrity through a distributed strain accommodation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a homogeneous single-phase alloy, the dual-phase alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly larger magnetic entropy change (ΔS) and adiabatic temperature change (ΔTad) at low fields, with reduced hysteresis in the magnetic response and maintained or improved mechanical stability and heat-exchange rates.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous rare‐earth‐free high‐entropy alloy produced without inducing nanoscale heterogeneity.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold for alloys with similar multi-principal element compositions (excluding rare earths) operating near room temperature and in low magnetic field regimes (up to ~1 T).
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the magnetocaloric enhancement, as well as the optimal scale of phase heterogeneity for balancing heat exchange and mechanical stability, remains uncertain and is likely to vary with the specific alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same rare‐earth‐free high‐entropy alloy composition: one set processed with rapid quenching (to promote nanoscale dual-phase heterogeneity) and a control set processed via slow cooling (yielding a more homogeneous single-phase structure). Characterize the microstructures by high-resolution TEM and XRD, then subject both sets of samples to low-field magnetocaloric measurements, thermal conductivity tests, and hysteresis loop assessments.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔS) under low (<1 T) applied fields
Thermal conductivity or heat exchange rate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly quenched (dual-phase) samples fail to demonstrate a significantly enhanced magnetocaloric effect (i.e., higher ΔS and ΔTad), lower magnetic hysteresis, and improved heat transfer without mechanical degradation compared to the homogeneous control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Magnetic and Transport Properties of New Dual-Phase High-Entropy Alloy FeRhIrPdPt

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are broadly explored from the perspective of mechanical, corrosion-resistance, catalytic, structural, superconducting, magnetic properties, and so on. In magnetic HEAs, 3d transition metals or rare-earth elements are well-studied compositional elements. We researched a magnetic HEA containing Fe combined with 4d and 5d transition metals, which has not been well investigated, and found a new dual-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) HEA FeRhIrPdPt. The structural, magnetic, and transport properties were evaluated by assuming that FeRhIrPdPt is a mixture of FeRh4, FeIr4, FePd4, and FePt4, all with the fcc structure. The dual-phase is composed of a Rh- and Ir-rich main phase and a Pd- and Pt-rich minor one. FeRh4 and FeIr4 show spin freezings at low temperatures, while FePd4 and FePt4 are ferromagnetic. Two magnetic features can characterize FeRhIrPdPt. One is the canonical spin-glass transition at 90 K, and the other is a ferromagnetic correlation that appears below 300 K.
